title: too much, too many and (not) enough
tagline: Too much noise, too many people, not enough time: say when something is a problem.
why: We use too when there is more than we want, and enough when the amount is right. They are in every complaint, every plan and every excuse: too tired, not enough time. Reading Parts 5 and 6 often test them in short gaps.

hook.text: Sofia and Mateo try to carry the boxes. "There are too many boxes!" says Sofia. "And they're too heavy," says Mateo. "We haven't got enough hands — or enough time!"
hook.ask: Find the problems in the story. Which words come before boxes, heavy and hands?

head: Pattern
Example
Note
rows: too tired to walk, old enough to drive

examples.text: There is too much noise in here.
examples.note: noise can't be counted → too much

examples.text: There are too many people in the lift.
examples.note: people can be counted → too many

examples.text: This bag is too heavy for me.
examples.note: more heavy than I can carry
so tired that I can't do it

examples.text: Is the room big enough for ten people?

examples.note: not enough = less than we need

watch_out.why: Friends can be counted, so use too many.
With an adjective, enough goes after it.

watch_out.wrong: He is too young for drive.
watch_out.why: Use to + the base verb, not for.
With a noun, enough goes before it.

watch_out.wrong: The soup is too much hot.
watch_out.why: Before an adjective use too, not too much.

l1.why: People can be counted, so use too many and are.
Spanish uses demasiado for everything. English uses too before an adjective.
Use to + verb, not para / for.

remember.trick: TOO is too much. ENOUGH is just right!
remember.tip: Too = a problem. Enough = the right amount, and not enough = a problem. Adjective + enough, but enough + noun.

dialogue.title: Packing for the school trip
dialogue.context: Miss Vega and the students check the bags before the school trip.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I think so. But there's too much bread and not enough fruit.

lines.speaker: Nadia

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Are the bottles big enough? It's a hot day.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega

can_do: I can say what is a problem with too much, too many and too + adjective.
I can say when the amount is right or wrong with enough and not enough.
I can use too tired to… and old enough to… to explain what I can or can't do.
summary: Too much + uncountable noun, too many + countable noun, too + adjective.
Enough goes before a noun (enough time) and after an adjective (big enough).
Not enough means less than you need.
Add to + verb: too tired to walk, old enough to drive.
